TASWIRA · AN ATLAS THROUGH TIME

Before the
borders.The land moved.

Follow the land that became Nigeria, from moving continents to the farmers, sculptors and ironworkers of Nok.

    Each block is one scene. Blocks are sized by reading time, not by years.

    Text version

    Everything on the map, scene by scene, with its sources. Built 2026-10-27. While the map plays, moving sparks, dust, light and ripples are decoration: only the dots, lines, colours and text carry information.

    Deep time: how the land was made (600 million to 5,000 years ago)

    Before there were people, the land itself moved. This chapter covers about 600 million years in a few minutes: the continents gather and break apart, a rift opens into West Africa and stops, the Niger Delta grows, and the Sahara turns green and dries again. If those 600 million years were one day, everything since the first Nok farmers would fit into its last half-second.

    How to read this map. The continents are drawn where a published plate model puts them (Merdith et al. 2021), on a globe with the grid of latitude and longitude of the time. The outlines are today's continents with their shelves, simplified, so they show where the land was, not the coastlines of the time. Rocks record how far from the poles they formed but not how far east or west, so the longitudes of deep time are the model's choice. The last two scenes are on the plain map of today's land, lakes and rivers.

    about 600 to 530 million years ago: Africa inside Gondwana

    About 600 million years ago, the rock that is now Nigeria lay inside a growing supercontinent called Gondwana. Between about 600 and 530 million years ago, mountain building welded its pieces together: South America, Africa, Antarctica, Arabia, India and Australia. Africa and South America sat side by side. Watch where Nigeria's rock goes from here.

    about 200 to 160 million years ago: Pangaea breaks up

    Gondwana had joined the northern continents into one supercontinent, Pangaea. About 200 million years ago, huge volcanic eruptions marked the start of its break-up, and the Central Atlantic opened between north-west Africa and North America. Between about 180 and 160 million years ago, Africa and Antarctica began to part.

    about 150 to 100 million years ago: The South Atlantic opens

    Then South America and Africa pulled apart like a zip opening from the south. The rift spread north from about 150 or 140 million years ago, and new ocean floor formed from about 135 to 130 million years ago. North of the equator, where Nigeria's coast is now, rifting began after about 120 million years ago and went on until about 100 million years ago.

    Disputed: Sources disagree on when the last land link broke: dinosaur footprints suggest some connection until about 120 million years ago, while rifting north of the equator went on until about 100 to 96 million years ago. The page shows the whole range.

    about 145 to 84 million years ago: A rift that stopped: the Benue Trough

    As the two continents parted, a third arm of the rift opened into Africa: the Benue Trough, about 1,000 km long, from the Bight of Benin to Lake Chad. It began to open at the start of the Cretaceous, about 145 million years ago, then stopped while the other two arms went on to become the South Atlantic. About 84 million years ago it was squeezed and folded. The Benue River runs along it today.

    around 70 million years ago: Coal swamps

    Around 70 million years ago, brackish marshes spread at the southern end of the trough, in the Anambra Basin. Their plants were buried and slowly became coal. It is the coal of the Udi Hills around Enugu, first shipped to Britain by 1914.

    about 56 million years ago to today: The Niger Delta grows

    From about 56 million years ago, at the start of the Eocene, the Niger and the Benue carried sand and mud to the sea where the arms of the old rift met. The delta has built out about 250 km to the south-west, over the ocean floor, and now covers some 300,000 km². Its sediment is more than 10 km thick, and it is still growing.

    • Niger Delta. Since the Eocene, which began about 56 million years ago, the Niger and Benue have carried sand and mud to the sea here. The delta has built out about 250 km to the south-west over the ocean floor, to some 300,000 km², with sediment more than 10 km thick. It sits where the arms of the old rift met. Evidence: Geology (government survey report). Location: A point on today's delta. The coast and rivers are drawn as they are today; when the delta began, the shore was further inland. How sure: Firm. Sources: Tertiary Niger Delta (Akata-Agbada) Petroleum System, Niger Delta Province (Open-File Report 99-50-H, chapter A), Eocene (Wikipedia).

    Sources: Tertiary Niger Delta (Akata-Agbada) Petroleum System, Niger Delta Province (Open-File Report 99-50-H, chapter A), Eocene (Wikipedia).

    about 14,500 to 5,000 years ago: A green Sahara, then the desert returns

    From about 14,500 years ago, stronger monsoon rains turned the Sahara green, with grassland, lakes and rivers, and Lake Chad grew into a vast Lake Mega-Chad. The rains weakened between about 6,000 and 5,000 years ago, in steps and at different times in different places. In the eastern Sahara, archaeology shows people leaving the drying desert for the Nile valley and moving south towards today's Sahel. South of Lake Chad, farming and herding villages spread from about 1800 BCE. Whether people from the drying desert moved there is not shown by the sources checked so far.

    • Lake Mega-Chad (Lake). In wet periods Lake Chad was far larger than today, and drained to the Benue and the Niger through the Mayo Kebbi. Halo or field: A disc of 330,000 km², the smaller of the two sizes given, centred on today's Lake Chad. The lake's real shoreline is not drawn. Evidence: Geology and climate studies (secondary sources). Location: Centred on today's Lake Chad. Disputed: Its size is given as about 330,000 km² in one source and about 400,000 km² in another. How sure: Disputed. Sources: African humid period (Wikipedia), Coordinates and facts for the deep-time chapter (Wikipedia place articles).

    Sources: African humid period (Wikipedia), Climate-Controlled Holocene Occupation in the Sahara: Motor of Africa's Evolution, Burial Practices, Settlement and Regional Connections around the Southern Lake Chad Basin, 1500 BC-AD 1500, Coordinates and facts for the deep-time chapter (Wikipedia place articles).

    Africa: peoples, cities and kingdoms (about 300,000 years ago to 1495 CE · overview, then rewind)

    A continental tour before the close-up. Each stop is a selected dated moment, not a claim about a whole kingdom’s duration. The last five views change geographic scale, then the story rewinds to Nok.

    How to read this map. Points locate sites or city centres with stated uncertainty, never empire outlines. Architecture is an original symbolic schematic, not a scale reconstruction or an emblem. Geography and the river locator are generalised modern physical references, not ancient coastlines, riverbanks or lake extents. Capital identifications and dates remain qualified. The tour explicitly jumps and rewinds; its progress rail shows scene order, not proportional years.

    About 300,000 years ago: Our species has an African story

    Rewind: the previous chapter ended around 5,000 years ago. Now we return to roughly 300,000 years ago. At Jebel Irhoud, early Homo sapiens remains were found with Middle Stone Age tools. This is one part of a much wider African story of human origins.

    • Jebel Irhoud · approximate locality. At Jebel Irhoud in present-day Morocco, early Homo sapiens remains occur with Middle Stone Age tools dated to about 300,000 years ago. This is one part of a much wider African story of human origins. Evidence: Archaeology and institutional/scholarly records. Location: Approximate fossil locality based on a nearby landmark, rounded to 31.87 N, 8.87 W. The 15 km overview halo is illustrative, not surveyed excavation accuracy. How sure: Approximate. Sources: The first of our kind, The age of the hominin fossils from Jebel Irhoud, Morocco, and the origins of the Middle Stone Age, Djebel Irhoud fossil locality 82672.

    Sources: The first of our kind, The age of the hominin fossils from Jebel Irhoud, Morocco, and the origins of the Middle Stone Age, Djebel Irhoud fossil locality 82672.

    Around 3100 BCE: A state takes shape on the Nile

    Jump forward by almost 300,000 years. Around 3100 BCE, the gradual unification of Upper and Lower Egypt reached a major stage. Memphis became a capital between the two regions.

    • Memphis · early Egypt (Kingdom). Around 3100 BCE, the gradual unification of Upper and Lower Egypt reached a major stage. Memphis became a capital between the two regions. Evidence: Archaeology and institutional/scholarly records. Location: UNESCO property component 86-001 representative point How sure: Approximate. Sources: Early Dynastic Period, Memphis and its Necropolis — Maps / geographical data.

    Sources: Early Dynastic Period, Memphis and its Necropolis — Maps / geographical data.

    Third century BCE: Kush builds its own royal landscape

    Further south on the Nile, Meroe was a major centre of Kush. In the third century BCE, royal burials here used steep-sided pyramids above underground tombs. The city and its royal cemeteries formed distinct parts of this landscape.

    • Meroe · royal cemeteries. Meroe was a major centre of Kush. From the third century BCE, most Kushite rulers were buried here. Its royal cemeteries used steep-sided pyramids above tombs cut into the ground. Schematic: Original symbolic steep-sided royal funerary pyramid with chapel. Represents the documented third-century BCE burial phase, not a measured or individually dated tomb. Evidence: Archaeology and institutional/scholarly records. Location: Representative point of the royal cemetery complex, separate from the royal city. It does not locate an individual pyramid footprint. How sure: Approximate. Sources: Archaeological Sites of the Island of Meroe, Archaeological Sites of the Island of Meroe — Nomination Text, Sudanese Cultural Heritage Sites.

    Sources: Archaeological Sites of the Island of Meroe, Archaeological Sites of the Island of Meroe — Nomination Text, Sudanese Cultural Heritage Sites.

    Around 200 BCE · within a longer urban sequence: A town without an invented king

    Shift west to the inland Niger delta. Djenné-Djenno grew from about 250 BCE. Archaeology reveals crafts, exchange and forms of self-government: an urban history alongside the stories of kings and courts.

    • Djenné-Djenno — ancient town. At Djenné-Djenno, a town grew in the inland Niger delta from about 250 BCE. Archaeology reveals crafts, exchange, and forms of self-government. Evidence: Archaeology and institutional/scholarly records. Location: Use a point with a broad site marker; no surveyed boundary or palace position established here. How sure: Approximate. Sources: Old Towns of Djenné, Sahel: Art and Empires on the Shores of the Sahara — Inside the Exhibition, Old Towns of Djenné — Maps, geographical data.

    Sources: Old Towns of Djenné, Sahel: Art and Empires on the Shores of the Sahara — Inside the Exhibition, Old Towns of Djenné — Maps, geographical data.

    Third–fourth centuries CE: Stone becomes architecture

    In north-eastern Africa, Aksum’s great stone stelae were carved in the third and fourth centuries CE. Some turned a single block of stone into the image of a many-storeyed building.

    • Aksum · stone stelae. Aksum's great stone stelae were carved in the third and fourth centuries CE. Some turned a single block of stone into the image of a many-storeyed building. Schematic: Original schematic monolith with architectural panels; class dated third/fourth century CE. Not an individual measured stele. Evidence: Archaeology and institutional/scholarly records. Location: UNESCO Aksum property representative point How sure: Approximate. Sources: Aksum, Aksum — Maps / geographical data.

    Sources: Aksum, Aksum — Maps / geographical data.

    Around 1100 CE · selected trade context: Gold, exchange and an uncertain capital

    Ghana, also called Wagadu, was linked to medieval gold exchange. Koumbi Saleh was a commercial centre; whether it was the capital remains debated. This earlier Ghana lay far from the present-day country of the same name.

    Disputed: The identification of Koumbi Saleh as Ghana’s political capital is debated. The scene locates the archaeological trading town, not a confirmed palace.

Location: Conservative illustrative radius, not measured survey error. UNESCO tentative entry supplies only a regional location. Disputed: Koumbi Saleh is a documented commercial centre. Identification as Ghana’s capital remains debated; this point does not locate a verified royal seat. How sure: Disputed.     Thirteenth century CE · regional overview: A centre east of Lake Chad

    Now east of Lake Chad. Kanem linked communities across the Sahara. Recent archaeological work considers Tié a probable location of Njimi, an early Islamic capital. The identification remains a research question as the regional story comes into focus.

    Disputed: Tié’s identification with Njimi is probable, not certain. No unverified capital point or medieval lake shoreline is drawn.

    Sources: The Lake Chad Region as a Crossroads: first archaeological and oral historical investigations into early Kanem-Borno and its intra-African connections, New Luminescence and Radiocarbon Dates for Kanem-Borno Fired-Brick Elite Sites in Kanem, Chad: Bayesian Chronological Modelling of Settlement Construction, Publication: Archaeological research in Tié, Chad.

    1324 CE · Musa’s pilgrimage: Mali, Musa and a city of learning

    In 1324, Mali’s ruler Musa travelled to Mecca through Cairo. His patronage helped Timbuktu develop as a centre of Islamic study. Timbuktu enters this tour as a commercial and scholarly city.

    • Mali — Musa's 1324 pilgrimage and Timbuktu. In 1324, Mali's ruler Musa travelled to Mecca through Cairo. His patronage helped Timbuktu develop as a centre of Islamic study. Evidence: Archaeology and institutional/scholarly records. Location: Property-level point, not a verified medieval palace, market stall, or exact initial mosque footprint. How sure: Approximate. Sources: Sahel: Art and Empires on the Shores of the Sahara — Inside the Exhibition, Timbuktu.

    Sources: Sahel: Art and Empires on the Shores of the Sahara — Inside the Exhibition, Timbuktu.

    Around 1400 CE · later building phase: A city built in stone

    Far to the south, Great Zimbabwe grew into a major trading city. Its fourteenth-century Great Enclosure shows the skill of its stone builders. The enclosure and conical tower form part of the site’s later architectural ensemble.

    • Great Zimbabwe · enclosure. In southern Africa, Great Zimbabwe grew into a major trading city. Its fourteenth-century Great Enclosure still expresses the skill of its stone builders. Schematic: Original enclosure-and-conical-tower schematic of the later architectural ensemble. The enclosure is dated to the fourteenth century; 1400 is an editorial snapshot, not a construction date for the individual tower. Evidence: Archaeology and institutional/scholarly records. Location: Representative site coordinate, rounded for an overview; not a surveyed boundary or a precise building footprint. Display halo is illustrative, not a measured confidence interval. How sure: Approximate. Sources: Great Zimbabwe National Monument, Great Zimbabwe National Monument — Maps / Geographical data.

    Sources: Great Zimbabwe National Monument, Great Zimbabwe National Monument — Maps / Geographical data.

    Thirteenth–fourteenth centuries CE: Africa faces the Indian Ocean too

    Turn toward the Indian Ocean. Kilwa Kisiwani flourished as a Swahili trading city in the thirteenth and fourteenth centuries. Its sea connections belong in Africa’s history alongside the Sahara and the Niger.

    • Kilwa Kisiwani · trading city. Kilwa Kisiwani was a Swahili trading city, especially prosperous in the thirteenth and fourteenth centuries. Its merchants connected African hinterland goods with Indian Ocean markets in Arabia, India and China. Evidence: Archaeology and institutional/scholarly records. Location: Kilwa Kisiwani component 144-001 representative point How sure: Approximate. Sources: Ruins of Kilwa Kisiwani and Ruins of Songo Mnara, Kilwa Kisiwani and Songo Mnara — Maps / geographical data.

    Sources: Ruins of Kilwa Kisiwani and Ruins of Songo Mnara, Kilwa Kisiwani and Songo Mnara — Maps / geographical data.

    1495 CE · monument at Gao: Gao and the Songhai world

    At Gao, a centre of Songhai, Askia Mohamed built an earthen monument in 1495. Trans-Saharan salt and gold exchange helped sustain the empire’s wealth. The city anchors our final stop before the camera pulls back.

    • Songhai — Gao and the Tomb of Askia. At Gao, capital of Songhai, Askia Mohamed built this earthen monument in 1495. Salt and gold exchange helped sustain the empire's wealth. Evidence: Archaeology and institutional/scholarly records. Location: Rounded periodic-report point is preferred because World Heritage webpage incorrectly gives east longitude; nomination independently specifies west. No precise boundary inferred. How sure: Approximate. Sources: Tomb of Askia, Tomb of Askia — Rapport Périodique Cycle 3, Section II.

    Sources: Tomb of Askia, Tomb of Askia — Rapport Périodique Cycle 3, Section II.

Sources: Reconnecting the Forest, Savanna, and Sahel in West Africa: The Sociopolitical Implications of a Long-Networked Past, Sahel: Art and Empires on the Shores of the Sahara — Inside the Exhibition, Migration Histories of the Medieval Afroeurasian Transition Zone: Aspects of Mobility between Africa, Asia and Europe, 300–1500 C.E..
    • Mali — Musa's 1324 pilgrimage and Timbuktu. In 1324, Mali's ruler Musa travelled to Mecca through Cairo. His patronage helped Timbuktu develop as a centre of Islamic study. Evidence: Archaeology and institutional/scholarly records. Location: Property-level point, not a verified medieval palace, market stall, or exact initial mosque footprint. How sure: Approximate. Sources: Sahel: Art and Empires on the Shores of the Sahara — Inside the Exhibition, Timbuktu.
    • Songhai — Gao and the Tomb of Askia. At Gao, capital of Songhai, Askia Mohamed built this earthen monument in 1495. Salt and gold exchange helped sustain the empire's wealth. Evidence: Archaeology and institutional/scholarly records. Location: Rounded periodic-report point is preferred because World Heritage webpage incorrectly gives east longitude; nomination independently specifies west. No precise boundary inferred. How sure: Approximate. Sources: Tomb of Askia, Tomb of Askia — Rapport Périodique Cycle 3, Section II.
    • Great Zimbabwe · enclosure. In southern Africa, Great Zimbabwe grew into a major trading city. Its fourteenth-century Great Enclosure still expresses the skill of its stone builders. Evidence: Archaeology and institutional/scholarly records. Location: Representative site coordinate, rounded for an overview; not a surveyed boundary or a precise building footprint. Display halo is illustrative, not a measured confidence interval. How sure: Approximate. Sources: Great Zimbabwe National Monument, Great Zimbabwe National Monument — Maps / Geographical data.

    Geographic interlude · different periods: Across sub-Saharan Africa

    Move south of the Sahara. This broad geographic view brings the Sahel, forest regions, eastern coast and southern cities into one frame. Then we narrow the view again toward West Africa.

    Geographic interlude · different periods: Follow the mapped Niger

    Now West Africa. The Niger begins in Guinea’s highlands, runs through the inland delta and bends across the western Sahel toward the Atlantic. Follow its broad sweep along this generalised physical locator, from the headwaters to the bend and the lower river.

Niger lake centreline bridges are shown only as narrow river locators, with no reservoir area or outline. How sure: Approximate.     Rewind · about 1500 BCE: Rewind to the first Nok chapter

    Our continental tour reached the medieval centuries. Now rewind to about 1500 BCE. We will follow the much earlier farmers, sculptors and ironworkers associated with Nok, then build the later regional story in order.

    • Nok village (Jaba LGA, Kaduna State). The first known Nok terracotta was found here in 1928, about 7 m deep in a tin mine. A second head, found nearby in 1943, led Bernard Fagg to recognise a lost sculptural tradition, and the culture is named after the village. Evidence: Documented chance finds, later studied by archaeologists. Location: Town location. The finds came from tin mines near the village. How sure: Firm. Sources: Nok culture (Wikipedia), Coordinates of Nok (Jaba LGA), Kagarko and Katsina-Ala (Wikipedia place articles).

    Sources: Nok culture (Wikipedia), Coordinates of Nok (Jaba LGA), Kagarko and Katsina-Ala (Wikipedia place articles).

    Nok: farmers, sculptors and early iron (about 1500 BCE to the turn of the era)

    The Nok culture lived in the hills and valleys of central Nigeria, roughly between today's Abuja, Kaduna and Jos. It is known from archaeology alone: no written records survive, so everything here comes from excavated sites and radiocarbon dates.

    about 1500 BCE to 1 CE: Where the Nok lived

    Archaeologists have found almost 500 Nok sites across central Nigeria and excavated 84 of them, with 270 radiocarbon dates. The four places on the map are ones named in the sources checked for this page. They are examples, not a full map of Nok sites.

    • Nok village (Jaba LGA, Kaduna State). The first known Nok terracotta was found here in 1928, about 7 m deep in a tin mine. A second head, found nearby in 1943, led Bernard Fagg to recognise a lost sculptural tradition, and the culture is named after the village. Evidence: Documented chance finds, later studied by archaeologists. Location: Town location. The finds came from tin mines near the village. How sure: Firm. Sources: Nok culture (Wikipedia), Coordinates of Nok (Jaba LGA), Kagarko and Katsina-Ala (Wikipedia place articles).
    • Janruwa, Janjala and Akura, near Kagarko. Three Nok sites about 1 km apart, excavated by the Frankfurt Nok project. They yielded pottery, terracotta fragments and plant remains used to study what Nok farmers grew. Evidence: Excavated (Frankfurt Nok project). Location: Placed at Kagarko town. The sites are near the town, not at this exact point. How sure: Firm. Sources: Exploring the Nok enigma, Coordinates of Nok (Jaba LGA), Kagarko and Katsina-Ala (Wikipedia place articles).
    • Taruga. A valley near the village of Takushara, excavated for eight days by Bernard Fagg in January 1961. Iron objects, slag, fragments of furnace blowpipes (tuyères) and pottery were found, and these finds led archaeologists to class the Nok culture as Iron Age. Evidence: Excavated (Fagg, 1961). Location: Rough. Placed 60 km south-east of Abuja from a written description, and could be 20 to 30 km out. The ring shows that uncertainty. Disputed: The date of Taruga's iron working is given as about 600 BCE in some histories, but Fagg's radiocarbon dates point to about the 4th to 3rd centuries BCE. The Frankfurt project places Nok iron working in the middle of the first millennium BCE. How sure: Disputed. Sources: Nok culture (Wikipedia), Taruga (Wikipedia), Development of complex societies in sub-Saharan Africa: The Nigerian Nok Culture (project results).
    • Katsina-Ala (Benue State). Terracotta heads and figures found here in the mid-20th century resemble Nok work. Fagg described them as a distinctive sub-style, far to the south-east of Nok village. Evidence: Chance finds described in secondary sources. Location: Town location. The exact find spots are not given in the sources checked. Disputed: Whether these are Nok proper or a related tradition is not settled in the sources checked. How sure: Disputed. Sources: Coordinates of Nok (Jaba LGA), Kagarko and Katsina-Ala (Wikipedia place articles).

    Sources: Development of complex societies in sub-Saharan Africa: The Nigerian Nok Culture (project results).

    about 1500 to 900 BCE: First farmers

    The earliest evidence of Nok farming dates to around 1500 BCE. Communities mainly grew millet. This phase is known from pottery and plant remains, not from sculpture: the terracottas came about six centuries later.

    • Janruwa, Janjala and Akura, near Kagarko. Three Nok sites about 1 km apart, excavated by the Frankfurt Nok project. They yielded pottery, terracotta fragments and plant remains used to study what Nok farmers grew. Evidence: Excavated (Frankfurt Nok project). Location: Placed at Kagarko town. The sites are near the town, not at this exact point. How sure: Firm. Sources: Exploring the Nok enigma, Coordinates of Nok (Jaba LGA), Kagarko and Katsina-Ala (Wikipedia place articles).

    Sources: Development of complex societies in sub-Saharan Africa: The Nigerian Nok Culture (project results), Professor Peter Breunig: The Significance of Nok Culture Sculptures in Nigerian Prehistory.

    about 900 to 400 BCE: Villages grow and sculpture begins

    Around 900 BCE settlements suddenly became much denser, and people began making large clay sculptures of human heads and figures. Many were deliberately broken and deposited, some near graves, at sites such as Pangwari and Ifana. Sculpture production seems to fall off sharply around 400 BCE.

A second head, found nearby in 1943, led Bernard Fagg to recognise a lost sculptural tradition, and the culture is named after the village. The sites are near the town, not at this exact point. How sure: Firm. Sources: Exploring the Nok enigma, Coordinates of Nok (Jaba LGA), Kagarko and Katsina-Ala (Wikipedia place articles).
    • Katsina-Ala (Benue State). Terracotta heads and figures found here in the mid-20th century resemble Nok work. Fagg described them as a distinctive sub-style, far to the south-east of Nok village. Evidence: Chance finds described in secondary sources. Location: Town location. The exact find spots are not given in the sources checked. Disputed: Whether these are Nok proper or a related tradition is not settled in the sources checked. How sure: Disputed. Sources: Coordinates of Nok (Jaba LGA), Kagarko and Katsina-Ala (Wikipedia place articles).

    Sources: Development of complex societies in sub-Saharan Africa: The Nigerian Nok Culture (project results), Professor Peter Breunig: The Significance of Nok Culture Sculptures in Nigerian Prehistory.

    middle of the 1st millennium BCE: Iron smelting

    In the later part of this phase, Nok people built furnaces and smelted iron, among the earliest iron working known in West Africa. Iron came a few centuries after the first terracottas, so the two should not be treated as one package. The exact dates are debated (see Taruga).

Location: Rough. Placed 60 km south-east of Abuja from a written description, and could be 20 to 30 km out. The ring shows that uncertainty. Disputed: The date of Taruga's iron working is given as about 600 BCE in some histories, but Fagg's radiocarbon dates point to about the 4th to 3rd centuries BCE. The Frankfurt project places Nok iron working in the middle of the first millennium BCE. How sure: Disputed. Sources: Nok culture (Wikipedia), Taruga (Wikipedia), Development of complex societies in sub-Saharan Africa: The Nigerian Nok Culture (project results).

The exact find spots are not given in the sources checked. Disputed: Whether these are Nok proper or a related tradition is not settled in the sources checked. How sure: Disputed.     Sources: Development of complex societies in sub-Saharan Africa: The Nigerian Nok Culture (project results), Professor Peter Breunig: The Significance of Nok Culture Sculptures in Nigerian Prehistory.

    about 400 BCE to the turn of the era: Decline

    After about 400 BCE, settlement activity fell sharply, and by the turn of the era the Nok culture disappears from the record. The sources checked do not give a settled explanation for why.

    1928 to 2021: Archaeological research and looting

    Tin-mining finds in 1928 and 1943 brought the sculptures to archaeologists' attention. Fagg excavated Taruga in 1961, and the Frankfurt project worked systematically from 2005 to 2021. When German researchers began looking for Nok sites from 1989, most of the ones they found had already been looted.

    Modern reference map: Today's map is used only to locate the archaeological sites. Its roads, towns and borders do not reconstruct the landscape of 1928 to 2021.

    From four regions to 36 states (1963 to 1996)

    Between 1967 and 1996, military governments redrew Nigeria's internal map five times, going from four regions to 36 states and a Federal Capital Territory. Each step is shown as a dated snapshot, not a smooth change.

    How to read this map. Each snapshot colours today's 36 states and the FCT by the state they belonged to on that date. That is an approximation: the 1967 and 1976 decrees defined states by older provinces, divisions and districts, and boundary commissions adjusted lines afterwards. Where one of today's states was split between earlier states, it is striped in its parents' colours. Thick lines are borders between states at that date. Faint dashed lines are today's borders.

    1963 to 1967: Four regions

    Before 1967, Nigeria's federation was made of large regions. A fourth, the Mid-Western Region, was carved out of the Western Region in 1963 (one source says 1964), and Lagos was a separate federal territory. The Northern Region alone covered about four-fifths of the country's land (79%, measured with today's state borders).

    Disputed: The Mid-Western Region is usually dated to 1963; the Forum of Federations chapter gives 1964.

    • Northern Region: today's Sokoto, Kebbi, Zamfara, Niger, Kaduna, Katsina, Kano, Jigawa, Borno, Yobe, Bauchi, Gombe, Adamawa, Taraba, Benue, Plateau, Nasarawa, Kwara, Kogi, FCT (Abuja).
    • Western Region: today's Oyo, Osun, Ogun, Ondo, Ekiti.
    • Mid-Western Region: today's Edo, Delta.
    • Eastern Region: today's Anambra, Enugu, Ebonyi, Imo, Abia, Rivers, Bayelsa, Cross River, Akwa Ibom.
    • Lagos (today): split between Federal Territory of Lagos and Western Region. Today's Lagos State joins the old Federal Territory of Lagos with mainland divisions of the Western Region.

    Sources: Federal Republic of Nigeria (in Constitutional Origins, Structure, and Change in Federal Countries).

    27 May 1967: Twelve states

    On 27 May 1967, General Yakubu Gowon's military government replaced the four regions with 12 states by decree. The decree described each state as a list of existing provinces, and set up a commission to settle boundaries.

    • North-Western: today's Sokoto, Kebbi, Zamfara, Niger.
    • North-Central: today's Kaduna, Katsina.
    • Kano: today's Kano, Jigawa.
    • North-Eastern: today's Borno, Yobe, Bauchi, Gombe, Adamawa, Taraba.
    • Benue-Plateau: today's Benue, Plateau, Nasarawa.
    • Kwara: today's Kwara.
    • Lagos: today's Lagos.
    • Western: today's Oyo, Osun, Ogun, Ondo, Ekiti.
    • Mid-Western: today's Edo, Delta.
    • East-Central: today's Anambra, Enugu, Ebonyi, Imo, Abia.
    • South-Eastern: today's Cross River, Akwa Ibom.
    • Rivers: today's Rivers, Bayelsa.
    • Kogi (today): split between Kwara and Benue-Plateau. Kogi was later made from parts of Kwara and Benue. One secondary source also names Niger, which came from North-Western. Disputed: Sources disagree on whether part of Kogi came from Niger (North-Western).
    • FCT (Abuja) (today): split between North-Western and Benue-Plateau. The FCT was later carved out of land in several northern states. Disputed: Sources disagree on which states gave land: commonly Niger, Plateau and Kwara; one list says Benue-Plateau, North-Central and North-Western. The 1976 states decree places the Abuja area in Niger.

    Sources: States (Creation and Transitional Provisions) Decree 1967, Decree No. 14, Federal Republic of Nigeria (in Constitutional Origins, Structure, and Change in Federal Countries), State-creation source check (agent review on issue #25).

    3 February 1976: Nineteen states and a new capital territory

    In 1976 General Murtala Mohammed's government created seven more states, making 19, and designated a Federal Capital Territory for a new capital at Abuja. Lagos stayed the capital for now. Mid-Western was renamed Bendel.

    • Sokoto: today's Sokoto, Kebbi, Zamfara.
    • Niger: today's Niger.
    • Kaduna: today's Kaduna, Katsina.
    • Kano: today's Kano, Jigawa.
    • Borno: today's Borno, Yobe.
    • Bauchi: today's Bauchi, Gombe.
    • Gongola: today's Adamawa, Taraba.
    • Plateau: today's Plateau, Nasarawa.
    • Benue: today's Benue.
    • Kwara: today's Kwara.
    • Lagos: today's Lagos.
    • Ogun: today's Ogun.
    • Oyo: today's Oyo, Osun.
    • Ondo: today's Ondo, Ekiti.
    • Bendel: today's Edo, Delta.
    • Anambra: today's Anambra, Enugu.
    • Imo: today's Imo, Abia.
    • Cross River: today's Cross River, Akwa Ibom.
    • Rivers: today's Rivers, Bayelsa.
    • Federal Capital Territory: today's FCT (Abuja).
    • Kogi (today): split between Kwara and Benue. Kogi was made in 1991 from parts of Kwara and Benue (one source also names Niger), so in 1976 it is shown as split between them. The review of the 1976 decree on issue #25 noted the Kogi area under Kwara; how much of today's Kogi was in Benue has not been checked against the decree's schedule. Disputed: Sources disagree on whether part of Kogi came from Niger, and the split line is not established.
    • Ebonyi (today): split between Anambra and Imo. Ebonyi was later made from parts of Enugu (then in Anambra) and Abia (then in Imo).

    Sources: States (Creation and Transitional Provisions) Decree 1976, Decree No. 12, Federal Republic of Nigeria (in Constitutional Origins, Structure, and Change in Federal Countries), List of Nigerian states by date of statehood (Wikipedia).

    23 September 1987: Twenty-one states

    On 23 September 1987, General Ibrahim Babangida's government created Katsina, from Kaduna, and Akwa Ibom, from Cross River.

    • Sokoto: today's Sokoto, Kebbi, Zamfara.
    • Niger: today's Niger.

    • Benue: today's Benue.
    • Kwara: today's Kwara.
    • Lagos: today's Lagos.
    • Ogun: today's Ogun.
    • Oyo: today's Oyo, Osun.
    • Ondo: today's Ondo, Ekiti.
    • Bendel: today's Edo, Delta.
    • Anambra: today's Anambra, Enugu.
    • Imo: today's Imo, Abia.
    • Cross River: today's Cross River.
    • Akwa Ibom: today's Akwa Ibom.
    • Rivers: today's Rivers, Bayelsa.
    • Federal Capital Territory: today's FCT (Abuja).
    • Kogi (today): split between Kwara and Benue. Still divided between Kwara and Benue until 1991 (one source also names Niger). Disputed: Sources disagree on whether part of Kogi came from Niger.
    • Ebonyi (today): split between Anambra and Imo. Still divided between Anambra and Imo.

    Sources: Katsina @30: a dream fulfilled, List of governors of Akwa Ibom State (Wikipedia).

    27 August 1991: Thirty states, and the capital moves

    On 27 August 1991, nine more states were created: Abia, Delta, Edo, Jigawa, Kebbi, Kogi, Osun, Taraba and Yobe. Gongola was renamed Adamawa, and Bendel was split into Edo and Delta. Later the same year the federal capital officially moved from Lagos to Abuja.

    Disputed: Secondary sources give the 1991 decree as either No. 37 or No. 41, so no decree number is shown.

    • Sokoto: today's Sokoto, Zamfara.

    Map key: how power and movement are drawn (examples from about 700 to 1903)

    A short preview of the map styles the later chapters will use. Before borders were surveyed, the region held kingdoms, walled city-states, trading networks, a caliphate of emirates and many self-governing communities, and each is drawn its own way rather than as coloured land. Trade, migration and war each move differently too. Every example is real and cited, but this is a key, not a story: the full chapters will add more places and checks.

    about 700 to 1380: Trade: salt across the Sahara

    Trade is drawn as a dotted route with the goods travelling along it. Caravans carried rock salt south from Bilma, in the Kawar oases, to the savanna north of Lake Chad, where Kanem's heartland lay. In return, enslaved people and ivory went north. This was the shortest crossing of the Sahara, on the road from Tripoli by way of Murzuk. Regular caravan routes across the desert grew from the 7th and 8th centuries. Around 1380 Kanem's rulers lost their capital and moved west across the lake to Bornu.

    • Bilma (Kawar oases). An oasis town where rock salt was mined for the caravan trade. Salt is still produced in its natron pans today. Evidence: Secondary sources (encyclopedia). Location: Town location. How sure: Firm. Sources: Trans-Saharan trade (Wikipedia), Coordinates and town facts for the map key (Wikipedia place articles).
    • Kanem (Kingdom). A kingdom whose heartland lay north-east of Lake Chad. It controlled trade routes to the north and exported salt, ivory, enslaved people and animal products. Evidence: Secondary sources (encyclopedia). Location: Rough. Kanem's first capital, probably Njimi, has never been located, so the marker sits at Mao, the main town of today's Kanem region of Chad, with a ring for the uncertainty. Disputed: Kanem's founding is usually dated to about 700 CE, but some sources give about 600 or about 900. How sure: Disputed. Sources: Kanem Empire (Wikipedia), Coordinates and town facts for the map key (Wikipedia place articles). Emblem: Nothing documented: Flags shown online for Kanem and Bornu have no source. The palm-tree flag shown for Kanem traces to the imaginary kingdom of "Organa" on 14th-century European maps. It is never used. How sure: Firm. Sources: List of Nigerian flags (Wikipedia), Catalan Atlas (Wikipedia).
    • Salt road from Bilma to Kanem. Trade route: Bilma (Kawar oases) to Kanem. Caravans carried rock salt south from Bilma to the savanna north of Lake Chad, and enslaved people and ivory went north in exchange. It was the shortest crossing of the Sahara, part of the road from Tripoli by way of Murzuk. Goods: rock salt. Evidence: Secondary sources (encyclopedia). Location: A line between the two places. The caravans' track across the dunes is not drawn. How sure: Firm. Sources: Trans-Saharan trade (Wikipedia).

    Sources: Trans-Saharan trade (Wikipedia), Kanem Empire (Wikipedia).

    15th century: City-states: the walled towns of the Hausa

    A city-state is drawn as a walled town with its own name. The Hausa states were separate kingdoms around fortified capitals, never one kingdom, so no shared border is drawn. By the 15th century Kano and Katsina were trading centres that competed with Bornu and Mali. A thin line joins two places only where tribute or an alliance is documented, with the arrow pointing to the overlord: Kano paid tribute to Bornu. Rano is left off because Kano had conquered it earlier, and Gobir, Zazzau and Biram wait until the sites of their 15th-century capitals are checked.

    • Daura (City-state). Remembered as the mother city of the Hausa states. Evidence: Oral tradition, in secondary sources. Location: Today's town of the same name. How sure: Approximate. Sources: Hausa Kingdoms (Wikipedia), Coordinates and town facts for the map key (Wikipedia place articles).
    • Katsina (City-state). A Hausa state around a walled city, believed to have been founded about 1100. By the 15th century it was a trading centre. Evidence: Secondary sources (encyclopedia). Location: Today's walled city of the same name. How sure: Approximate. Sources: Hausa Kingdoms (Wikipedia), Coordinates and town facts for the map key (Wikipedia place articles).
    • Kano (City-state). A Hausa state around a walled city. By the Kano Chronicle's dating its walls were begun under Gijimasu (1095 to 1134). Evidence: Secondary sources; the Kano Chronicle's early dates are reconstructions. Location: Today's old city of Kano. How sure: Approximate. Sources: Hausa Kingdoms (Wikipedia), Coordinates and town facts for the map key (Wikipedia place articles).
    • Ngazargamu (Bornu) (Kingdom). Founded about 1472 as the first substantial capital of Bornu, the kingdom that grew from Kanem, in the fork of two rivers near today's Geidam. It was captured and destroyed in 1808. Evidence: Ruins, and secondary sources. Location: The ruined city's location. How sure: Approximate. Sources: Bornu Empire (Wikipedia), Coordinates and town facts for the map key (Wikipedia place articles). Emblem: Nothing documented: Flags shown online for Kanem and Bornu have no source. The palm-tree flag shown for Kanem traces to the imaginary kingdom of "Organa" on 14th-century European maps. It is never used. How sure: Firm. Sources: List of Nigerian flags (Wikipedia), Catalan Atlas (Wikipedia).
    • Kano's tribute to Bornu. Tribute, from Kano to Ngazargamu (Bornu). Bornu was recognised as Kano's overlord and paid tribute. Evidence: Secondary sources (encyclopedia). Disputed: One source says Bornu made the Hausa states its vassals in the 15th century, with tribute sent through Daura, but is unsure whether this covered all of them or only Kano and Biram. Another names only Kano. How sure: Disputed. Sources: Hausa Kingdoms (Wikipedia), Bornu Empire (Wikipedia).

    Sources: Hausa Kingdoms (Wikipedia), Bornu Empire (Wikipedia).

    15th century onward: Migration: Fulani into Hausaland and Bornu

    Migration is drawn as a soft band of drifting dots with no arrowhead, because people moved over generations rather than marching on a target. By the 15th century there was a steady flow of Fulani into Hausaland, and later into Bornu. Some were herders who moved with their cattle through the year, and others settled in towns, so the band runs through the Hausa towns instead of forming a country of its own. Where the Fulani came from is unclear, so the band fades out at its western end.

    • Katsina (City-state). A Hausa state around a walled city, believed to have been founded about 1100. By the 15th century it was a trading centre. Evidence: Secondary sources (encyclopedia). Location: Today's walled city of the same name. How sure: Approximate. Sources: Hausa Kingdoms (Wikipedia), Coordinates and town facts for the map key (Wikipedia place articles).
    • Kano (City-state). A Hausa state around a walled city. By the Kano Chronicle's dating its walls were begun under Gijimasu (1095 to 1134). Evidence: Secondary sources; the Kano Chronicle's early dates are reconstructions. Location: Today's old city of Kano. How sure: Approximate. Sources: Hausa Kingdoms (Wikipedia), Coordinates and town facts for the map key (Wikipedia place articles).
    • Ngazargamu (Bornu) (Kingdom). Founded about 1472 as the first substantial capital of Bornu, the kingdom that grew from Kanem, in the fork of two rivers near today's Geidam. It was captured and destroyed in 1808. Evidence: Ruins, and secondary sources. Location: The ruined city's location. How sure: Approximate. Sources: Bornu Empire (Wikipedia), Coordinates and town facts for the map key (Wikipedia place articles). Emblem: Nothing documented: Flags shown online for Kanem and Bornu have no source. The palm-tree flag shown for Kanem traces to the imaginary kingdom of "Organa" on 14th-century European maps. It is never used. How sure: Firm. Sources: List of Nigerian flags (Wikipedia), Catalan Atlas (Wikipedia).
    • Fulani moving into Hausaland and Bornu. Migration: Katsina to Kano to Ngazargamu (Bornu). By the 15th century there was a steady flow of Fulani into Hausaland, and later into Bornu. Some were herders who moved with their cattle through the year, some were semi-nomadic, and others lived permanently in towns. When: by the 15th century, then into Bornu. Uncertain part of the route: start. Evidence: Secondary sources, partly resting on oral tradition. Location: Drawn through Katsina and Kano to Ngazargamu to stand for Hausaland and Bornu. People moved over a wide area and many generations, not along one route. Disputed: Where the Fulani came from is unclear. Language evidence points to Futa Toro in the Senegal valley, and one estimate, mainly from oral tradition, has migrants leaving it for the east between the 11th and 14th centuries. How sure: Disputed. Sources: Fula people (Wikipedia), Hausa Kingdoms (Wikipedia).

    Sources: Fula people (Wikipedia), Hausa Kingdoms (Wikipedia).

    1440 to about 1600: A kingdom: Benin

    A kingdom is drawn as its capital with a soft halo of influence that fades with distance, never as a hard border. In 1440 Ewuare came to power at Edo, today's Benin City, and expanded what had been a city-state. From the mid-15th century Benin's armies pushed west into eastern Yorubaland, and its influence reached Lagos by about the mid-1500s. The Niger seems to have been the eastern limit of its rule. The badge is the leopard, one of the principal symbols of the Oba in Benin art. It is drawn as a royal symbol, not a flag, because no flag of the kingdom is documented.

    • Edo (Benin City) (Kingdom). Capital of the Kingdom of Benin, ruled by the Oba. Ewuare came to power in 1440 and expanded the former city-state. Halo or field: Rough. Benin's influence reached Lagos, about 250 km to the west, by about the mid-1500s, while the Niger, about 130 km to the east, seems to have been the limit of its rule. A circle cannot show that shape, so the halo only says that influence faded with distance. Evidence: Secondary sources (encyclopedia). Location: Today's Benin City. How sure: Firm. Sources: Kingdom of Benin (Wikipedia), Coordinates and town facts for the map key (Wikipedia place articles). Emblem: Symbol, not a flag: The leopard, one of the principal symbols of the Oba in Benin court art. Coral-bead regalia, mudfish and ivory trumpets also mark kingship. A royal symbol, not a flag: no flag of the kingdom is documented. Drawn as a plain silhouette, not copied from objects taken in 1897. The source checked does not date the leopard imagery. How sure: Approximate. Sources: Benin court and ceremonial art (Wikipedia).

    Sources: Kingdom of Benin (Wikipedia), Benin court and ceremonial art (Wikipedia).

    about 1640 to 1901: A network: the Aro

    A network is drawn as threads from its centre, with no area filled in, because the Aro did not rule a territory. From Arochukwu, home of the Ibini Ukpabi oracle, the Aro traded with the monarchies of Onitsha and Oguta, among others. Enslaved people were sold at markets including Oguta Lake, Onitsha and Bonny, and the confederacy's economy rested mainly on enslaved people and palm oil. Neighbouring groups such as the Ohafia, Edda and Abam fought as its allies. British forces took Arochukwu on 28 December 1901, and the confederacy collapsed by early 1902.

    • Arochukwu (Centre of a network). Centre of the Aro Confederacy and home of the Ibini Ukpabi oracle, with the Aro king and a central council. Evidence: Secondary sources (encyclopedia). Location: Today's town of the same name. How sure: Approximate. Sources: Aro Confederacy (Wikipedia), Coordinates and town facts for the map key (Wikipedia place articles). Emblem: Nothing documented: A flag with crowns, a musket and a lance is shown online without a source. It may be a modern community flag. Nothing is drawn until its origin is checked. How sure: To check. Sources: List of Nigerian flags (Wikipedia).
    • Onitsha (Kingdom). A town on the Niger with kings called the Obi. Evidence: Secondary sources (encyclopedia). Location: Today's town of the same name. Disputed: Onitsha's founding is dated to between 1630 and 1680 by one source, and to the 16th century by others. How sure: Disputed. Sources: Igbo people (Wikipedia), Coordinates and town facts for the map key (Wikipedia place articles).
    • Oguta (Kingdom). A monarchy on Oguta Lake that traded with the Aro; enslaved people were sold at a market there. Evidence: Secondary sources (encyclopedia). Location: Today's town on the eastern bank of Oguta Lake. How sure: Approximate. Sources: Aro Confederacy (Wikipedia), Coordinates and town facts for the map key (Wikipedia place articles).
    • Bonny (City-state). A port kingdom and one of the main trading towns of the coast. Enslaved people were sold there, and after Britain abolished its slave trade in 1807 the port turned to palm oil, ivory and pepper. Evidence: Secondary sources (encyclopedia). Location: Today's town on Bonny Island. How sure: Firm. Sources: Aro Confederacy (Wikipedia), Coordinates and town facts for the map key (Wikipedia place articles).
    • Aro trade with Onitsha. Trade, from Arochukwu to Onitsha. The Aro traded with the Onitsha monarchy, and enslaved people were sold at Onitsha. Evidence: Secondary sources (encyclopedia). How sure: Firm. Sources: Aro Confederacy (Wikipedia).
    • Aro trade with Oguta. Trade, from Arochukwu to Oguta. The Aro traded with the Oguta monarchy, and enslaved people were sold at Oguta Lake. Evidence: Secondary sources (encyclopedia). How sure: Firm. Sources: Aro Confederacy (Wikipedia).
    • Aro trade through Bonny. Trade, from Arochukwu to Bonny. Bonny was one of the markets where enslaved people from the Aro trade were sold. Evidence: Secondary sources (encyclopedia). How sure: Firm. Sources: Aro Confederacy (Wikipedia).

    Sources: Aro Confederacy (Wikipedia).

    19th century, before colonial rule: Self-governing communities: Igbo towns and villages

    Self-governing communities are drawn as a field of small dots with no capital and no edge. Most Igbo communities were run by assemblies and councils of elders, built on patrilineages called umunna, and many towns were also partly governed by the Ozo title society. There was no single Igbo kingdom, so none is drawn. A few places did have kings: Onitsha's were called the Obi, and Nri and Arochukwu had priest-kings.

    • Igbo communities (Self-governing communities). Most Igbo communities were run by assemblies and councils of elders, built on patrilineages called umunna, and many towns were also partly governed by the Ozo title society. Halo or field: The dotted field is centred roughly on Igboland east of the Niger. It is a pattern, not a map of villages, and its edge is not a border. Evidence: Secondary sources (encyclopedia). Location: Rough area only. How sure: Approximate. Sources: Igbo people (Wikipedia). Emblem: Nothing documented: No emblem is documented in the sources checked for the communities represented here. Ichi facial marks showed status, not political rule, and are not used as decoration. How sure: Firm. Sources: Kingdom of Nri (Wikipedia).
    • Onitsha (Kingdom). A town on the Niger with kings called the Obi. Evidence: Secondary sources (encyclopedia). Location: Today's town of the same name. Disputed: Onitsha's founding is dated to between 1630 and 1680 by one source, and to the 16th century by others. How sure: Disputed. Sources: Igbo people (Wikipedia), Coordinates and town facts for the map key (Wikipedia place articles).

    Sources: Igbo people (Wikipedia).

    1809 to 1903: A caliphate of emirates: Sokoto

    A caliphate is drawn as the caliph's seat with a line from each emirate, showing allegiance rather than one border. The jihad that began in 1804 brought the Hausa states under new emirates: Zaria was captured in 1805 and Kano in 1807. Sokoto was founded as a military camp in 1809 and became the caliph's seat, and Gwandu became a co-capital from which the western and southern lands were overseen. Each emir was appointed by the caliph and governed with wide self-rule, travelling every year to pledge allegiance and bring tribute in crops, cowries and enslaved people.

    • Sokoto (Seat of the caliphate). Founded as a military camp in 1809, and the seat of the caliph, the Amir al-Mu'minin. Evidence: Secondary sources (encyclopedia). Location: Today's city of Sokoto. How sure: Firm. Sources: Sokoto Caliphate (Wikipedia), Coordinates and town facts for the map key (Wikipedia place articles). Emblem: Nothing documented: Flags circulate online, but no source for any design has been found. Nothing is drawn until a description from the time or a surviving banner is found, for example in travellers' accounts such as Clapperton's or Barth's. How sure: To check.
    • Gwandu (Seat of the caliphate). A co-capital of the caliphate, from which its emirs oversaw the western and southern lands. Other towns served as the western capital in some years. Evidence: Secondary sources (encyclopedia). Location: Today's town of Gwandu. How sure: Firm. Sources: Sokoto Caliphate (Wikipedia), Coordinates and town facts for the map key (Wikipedia place articles). Emblem: Nothing documented: Flags circulate online, but no source for any design has been found. Nothing is drawn until a description from the time or a surviving banner is found, for example in travellers' accounts such as Clapperton's or Barth's. How sure: To check.
    • Katsina (Emirate). The emirate set up in Katsina after the jihad. Evidence: Secondary sources (encyclopedia). Location: The walled city of Katsina. How sure: Firm. Sources: Sokoto Caliphate (Wikipedia), Coordinates and town facts for the map key (Wikipedia place articles).
    • Kano (Emirate). The emirate set up after jihad forces captured Kano in 1807. Evidence: Secondary sources (encyclopedia). Location: The old city of Kano. How sure: Firm. Sources: Sokoto Caliphate (Wikipedia), Coordinates and town facts for the map key (Wikipedia place articles).
    • Zaria (Emirate). Zaria, capital of Zazzau, was captured by the Fulani in 1805 during the jihad. Evidence: Secondary sources (encyclopedia). Location: Today's city of Zaria. How sure: Firm. Sources: Sokoto Caliphate (Wikipedia), Coordinates and town facts for the map key (Wikipedia place articles).
    • Katsina's allegiance to Sokoto. Allegiance, from Katsina to Sokoto. Katsina's emir recognised the caliph at Sokoto as overlord, and travelled each year to pledge allegiance and bring tribute. Evidence: Secondary sources (encyclopedia). How sure: Firm. Sources: Sokoto Caliphate (Wikipedia).
    • Kano's allegiance to Sokoto. Allegiance, from Kano to Sokoto. Kano's emir recognised the caliph at Sokoto as overlord, and travelled each year to pledge allegiance and bring tribute. Evidence: Secondary sources (encyclopedia). How sure: Firm. Sources: Sokoto Caliphate (Wikipedia).
    • Zazzau's allegiance to Sokoto. Allegiance, from Zaria to Sokoto. Zazzau's emir recognised the caliph at Sokoto as overlord, and travelled each year to pledge allegiance and bring tribute. Evidence: Secondary sources (encyclopedia). How sure: Firm. Sources: Sokoto Caliphate (Wikipedia).

    Sources: Sokoto Caliphate (Wikipedia), Coordinates and town facts for the map key (Wikipedia place articles).

    1 January 1900: Claimed on paper: the protectorates of 1900

    A claim on paper is drawn as hatching, and it turns solid only where occupation is documented. On 1 January 1900 the Royal Niger Company handed its territories to the British government for £865,000, and with the Niger Coast Protectorate they became the Protectorates of Northern and Southern Nigeria. On paper, Sokoto, Kano and Zaria were now inside a British protectorate. On the ground, the caliph and the emirs still governed them.

    • Sokoto (Seat of the caliphate). Founded as a military camp in 1809, and the seat of the caliph, the Amir al-Mu'minin. Colonial claim: claimed on paper (hatched). Evidence: Secondary sources (encyclopedia). Location: Today's city of Sokoto. How sure: Firm. Sources: Sokoto Caliphate (Wikipedia), Coordinates and town facts for the map key (Wikipedia place articles). Emblem: Nothing documented: Flags circulate online, but no source for any design has been found. Nothing is drawn until a description from the time or a surviving banner is found, for example in travellers' accounts such as Clapperton's or Barth's. How sure: To check.
    • Kano (Emirate). The emirate set up after jihad forces captured Kano in 1807. Colonial claim: claimed on paper (hatched). Evidence: Secondary sources (encyclopedia). Location: The old city of Kano. How sure: Firm. Sources: Sokoto Caliphate (Wikipedia), Coordinates and town facts for the map key (Wikipedia place articles).
    • Zaria (Emirate). Zaria, capital of Zazzau, was captured by the Fulani in 1805 during the jihad. Colonial claim: claimed on paper (hatched). Evidence: Secondary sources (encyclopedia). Location: Today's city of Zaria. How sure: Firm. Sources: Sokoto Caliphate (Wikipedia), Coordinates and town facts for the map key (Wikipedia place articles).

    Sources: Royal Niger Company (Wikipedia), Battle of Kano (Wikipedia), Coordinates and town facts for the map key (Wikipedia place articles).

    1901 to March 1903: A campaign: Zaria, Kano and Sokoto taken

    A military campaign is drawn as a hard arrow, timed to each dated stop. As each town is taken, its hatching turns solid. British forces took Zaria in 1901. A force under Colonel Thomas Morland left Zaria at the end of January 1903 and took Kano on 3 February after heavy fighting. In March British forces reached Sokoto, which fell after a battle on 15 March. Caliph Attahiru I left the city, and was killed later in 1903.

    Disputed: Attahiru I's death is dated to June 1903 in one source and to the Battle of Burmi on 27 July 1903 in others.

Evidence: Secondary sources (encyclopedia). Location: Today's city of Zaria. How sure: Firm. Sources: Sokoto Caliphate (Wikipedia), Coordinates and town facts for the map key (Wikipedia place articles).

Evidence: Secondary sources (encyclopedia). Location: Today's city of Sokoto. How sure: Firm.     • British campaign from Zaria to Kano and Sokoto. Military campaign: Zaria (approx. taken 1901 (year only)) to Kano (3 Feb 1903) to Sokoto (15 Mar 1903). British forces took Zaria in 1901. A force under Colonel Thomas Morland left Zaria at the end of January 1903 and took Kano on 3 February. British forces under Kemball and Morland then took Sokoto after a battle on 15 March. Evidence: Secondary sources (encyclopedia). Location: Straight lines join the towns in the order they were taken. The columns' routes are not shown, and the line from Kano to Sokoto stands for the British advance, not one column's march.     Flags, emblems and symbols

    What is documented for each actor. A flag or symbol is drawn only from a cited description; where nothing is documented, nothing is invented.

    • Royal Niger Company. Flag (1887 to 1899): Badge: a black Y for the Niger, the Benue and their joined course to the sea, with ARS, JUS and PAX in yellow on its arms, inside a red ring on white. Flown on a White Ensign from 2 June 1887, then on a Blue Ensign from 1 February 1888. Its use until 1899 is presumed, not documented. How sure: Approximate. Sources: Royal Niger Company (Flags of the World).
    • Lagos Colony, the Oil Rivers and Niger Coast Protectorates, Northern and Southern Nigeria. Nothing documented: Badges existed and are listed by flag reference sites. No source checked so far describes them, so none is drawn yet. How sure: To check.
    • Colony and Protectorate of Nigeria. Flag (1914 to 1952): Blue Ensign with a red disc holding a green six-pointed star around a crown, with "Nigeria" below. Lugard wrote in 1940 that he first suggested the star design, for Northern Nigeria. A change to St Edward's Crown after 1953 is a theory, and one writer is not sure those versions flew, so they are not used. How sure: Firm. Sources: List of Nigerian flags (Wikipedia), Colonial Nigeria (Flags of the World).
    • Nana Olomu (Itsekiri), at Ebrohimi. Flag ( to 1894): Two personal flags, both made before 1894. One is red with a printed Union Flag in the corner and NANNA in white. The other is yellow with an upside-down Union Flag, NANNA in blue and a painted man shooting a leopard; it was captured in 1894. Local images next to a printed Union Flag: the mix says something about delta politics in the 1880s. How sure: Firm. Sources: Royal Museums Greenwich, object 556, Royal Museums Greenwich, object 555.
    • Unknown owner, probably Itsekiri. Flag: Red, with white figures of one man beheading another. Said to have been brought back from the 1897 Benin expedition. Disputed: Its maker, owner and meaning are unknown. It is shown only as an unidentified flag, never as Benin's. How sure: Disputed. Sources: Royal Museums Greenwich, object 557, Unidentified flag from the Kingdom of Benin (Wikipedia).
    • Kingdom of Benin. Symbol, not a flag: The leopard, one of the principal symbols of the Oba in Benin court art. Coral-bead regalia, mudfish and ivory trumpets also mark kingship. A royal symbol, not a flag: no flag of the kingdom is documented. Drawn as a plain silhouette, not copied from objects taken in 1897. The source checked does not date the leopard imagery. How sure: Approximate. Sources: Benin court and ceremonial art (Wikipedia).
    • Yoruba kingdoms (Ife, Oyo and their successors). Symbol, not a flag: The interlaced Solomon's knot, commonly viewed as a royal symbol among the Yoruba. No flag is documented. How sure: Firm. Sources: Nigerian heraldry (Wikipedia).
    • Hausa states. Symbol, not a flag: The Dagin Arewa, a star-shaped northern knot used in building, design and embroidery. Its age is not known from the sources checked, so it is not yet placed in any century. No city flags are documented. How sure: To check. Sources: Nigerian heraldry (Wikipedia).
    • Sokoto Caliphate. Nothing documented: Flags circulate online, but no source for any design has been found. Nothing is drawn until a description from the time or a surviving banner is found, for example in travellers' accounts such as Clapperton's or Barth's. How sure: To check.
    • Kanem and Bornu. Nothing documented: Flags shown online for Kanem and Bornu have no source. The palm-tree flag shown for Kanem traces to the imaginary kingdom of "Organa" on 14th-century European maps. It is never used. How sure: Firm. Sources: List of Nigerian flags (Wikipedia), Catalan Atlas (Wikipedia).
    • Aro Confederacy. Nothing documented: A flag with crowns, a musket and a lance is shown online without a source. It may be a modern community flag. Nothing is drawn until its origin is checked. How sure: To check. Sources: List of Nigerian flags (Wikipedia).
    • Nri and Igbo communities. Nothing documented: No emblem is documented in the sources checked for the communities represented here. Ichi facial marks showed status, not political rule, and are not used as decoration. How sure: Firm. Sources: Kingdom of Nri (Wikipedia).
    • Biafra. Flag (1967 to 1970): Red, black and green stripes with a golden rising sun of eleven rays, one for each province, over a gold bar. First raised on 30 May 1967, taken from the Eastern Region's arms. How sure: Firm. Sources: Flag of Biafra (Wikipedia).
    • Nigeria. Flag (1960 to today): Green-white-green, designed by Michael Taiwo Akinkunmi and chosen in 1959 from almost 3,000 entries. His red sun was removed. Raised at midnight on 1 October 1960. How sure: Firm. Sources: Flag of Nigeria (Wikipedia).

    • Gondwana (Wikipedia). Wikipedia contributors, accessed 2026. encyclopedia (secondary, used as a pointer to the works it cites). Use and rights: CC BY-SA 4.0 text; facts cited only, no text reused. What was checked: Opened 27 Oct 2026. Assembly c. 800 to 650 Ma (East African Orogeny) to c. 600 to 530 Ma (Brasiliano and Kuunga orogenies); remnants include South America, Africa, Antarctica, Australia, Zealandia, Arabia and India; Pangaea's break-up began with the Central Atlantic magmatic province, peaking c. 200 Ma; Africa and Antarctica began to part c. 180 to 160 Ma; South Atlantic rifting propagated north c. 150 or 140 Ma, spreading c. 135 to 130 Ma, rifting north of the equator after 120.4 Ma until c. 100 to 96 Ma; footprints suggest a land link as late as the early Aptian (c. 120 Ma); 'considerable debate over the exact timing'.
    • Benue Trough (Wikipedia). Wikipedia contributors, accessed 2026. encyclopedia (secondary, used as a pointer to the works it cites). Use and rights: CC BY-SA 4.0 text; facts cited only, no text reused. What was checked: Opened 27 Oct 2026. About 1,000 km north-east from the Bight of Benin to Lake Chad, about 150 km wide, its southern limit the northern edge of the Niger Delta; rifting began at the start of the Cretaceous (145 Ma); intense compression and folding in the Santonian, about 84 Ma; commonly explained as an aulacogen, the inactive arm of a three-armed rift as South America separated from Africa; coal swamps in the Anambra Basin; the Enugu deposits formed in brackish marshes in the Late Campanian to early Maastrichtian, around 70 Ma. No specific date for the start of rifting beyond 'the start of the Cretaceous' (the outline's 118 Ma is not supported).
    • Tertiary Niger Delta (Akata-Agbada) Petroleum System, Niger Delta Province (Open-File Report 99-50-H, chapter A). Michele L. W. Tuttle, Michael E. Brownfield and Ronald R. Charpentier, US Geological Survey, 1999. government geological report (secondary). Use and rights: US government work, public domain; facts cited. What was checked: Opened 27 Oct 2026. The delta proper began developing in the Eocene; from the Eocene to the present it has prograded south-west about 250 km over oceanic crust into the Gulf of Guinea; area some 300,000 km²; sediments over 10 km thick in the depocentre; the Benue-Abakaliki trough is a failed arm of a rift triple junction associated with the opening of the South Atlantic.
    • Eocene (Wikipedia). Wikipedia contributors, accessed 2026. encyclopedia (geological time scale). Use and rights: CC BY-SA 4.0 text; facts cited only, no text reused. What was checked: Opened 27 Oct 2026. The Eocene began about 56 million years ago and ended between 33.9 and 33.4 Ma.
    • African humid period (Wikipedia). Wikipedia contributors, accessed 2026. encyclopedia (secondary, used as a pointer to the works it cites). Use and rights: CC BY-SA 4.0 text; facts cited only, no text reused. What was checked: Opened 27 Oct 2026. Began about 14,600 to 14,500 years ago and ended 6,000 to 5,000 years ago, apparently in several steps and at different times in different places; Lake Megachad about 330,000 km²; humans gradually abandoned the desert for places with more secure water, such as the Nile valley. It does not say that people moved south towards the Niger or Lake Chad.
    • Climate-Controlled Holocene Occupation in the Sahara: Motor of Africa's Evolution. Rudolph Kuper and Stefan Kröpelin, Science 313, 803-807, 2006. peer-reviewed article (archaeology and climate). Use and rights: Cited and described; no text or figures reused. What was checked: Opened 27 Oct 2026 (author copy at the University of Cologne). About the eastern Sahara (Egypt, Sudan and adjacent Libya and Chad): humid from 8500 to 5300 BCE; regular rains stopped reaching the Egyptian Sahara by 5300 BCE and full desert returned about 3500 BCE; people moved to the Nile valley and ecological refuges, and towards today's Sahel and the Sudanese plains. The authors suggest the process applied to the whole Sahara, an inference rather than a finding for the central and western Sahara.

C. Gatto, D. J. Mattingly, N. Ray and M. Sterry (Cambridge University Press), 2019. book chapter (archaeology); only the summary was read. Use and rights: Cited and described; no text reused. The full chapter is not open access. What was checked: Chapter page opened 27 Oct 2026; only its summary was read. From c. 1800 BC agro-pastoral systems developed and permanent settlements expanded south of Lake Chad, first on Gajiganna Culture sites; environmental change involved periodic population exchanges between the southern Sahara and the Lake Chad Basin.
